notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Rainfall is precipitation in the form of liquid water drops falling from clouds.
  • It is one of the most important elements of India's climate.
  • India's rainfall is highly seasonal, uneven and variable.
  • Most regions receive a major share of annual rainfall during the monsoon months.
  • Rainfall distribution strongly affects agriculture, rivers, reservoirs, groundwater and natural vegetation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

India's Rainfall → Seasonal + Uneven + Variable

2. Precipitation
  • Precipitation is any form of water falling from the atmosphere to Earth's surface.
  • Major forms include:
  • Rain.
  • Snow.
  • Sleet.
  • Hail.
  • Rain is the dominant form of precipitation over most of India.
3. Conditions Necessary for Rainfall

Rainfall generally requires:

  • Moisture in the atmosphere.
  • Cooling of moist air.
  • Condensation.
  • Formation and growth of cloud droplets.
  • Droplets becoming heavy enough to fall.
4. Condensation
  • Condensation is the conversion of water vapour into liquid water.
  • It occurs when moist air cools sufficiently.
  • Condensation forms cloud droplets.
  • Dust, salt and other tiny particles act as condensation nuclei.
5. Dew Point
  • Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated with water vapour.
  • Cooling air to its dew point can lead to condensation.
  • Higher moisture content generally produces a higher dew point.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dew Point → Air Saturation Temperature

6. Saturation
  • Saturated air contains the maximum amount of water vapour possible at a given temperature.
  • Warm air can generally hold more water vapour than cold air.
  • Cooling therefore increases relative humidity.
7. Relative Humidity
  • Relative humidity compares the actual amount of water vapour in air with the maximum it can hold at that temperature.
  • It is expressed as a percentage.
  • Relative humidity rises as air cools if its moisture content remains unchanged.
8. Main Types of Rainfall

Rainfall is commonly classified into:

  • Convectional rainfall.
  • Orographic rainfall.
  • Cyclonic or frontal rainfall.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rainfall Types → Convectional + Orographic + Cyclonic

9. Convectional Rainfall
  • Strong heating warms air near the surface.
  • Warm air becomes lighter and rises.
  • Rising air expands and cools.
  • Condensation produces clouds and rainfall.
  • Such rainfall is often intense and short-lived.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Surface Heating → Convection → Rain

10. Convectional Rainfall in India
  • Convectional showers occur especially during hot weather.
  • Pre-monsoon thunderstorms are common examples.
  • They often occur during afternoons and evenings.
11. Orographic Rainfall
  • Moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier.
  • Rising air cools and condenses.
  • Heavy rainfall occurs on the windward side.
  • Descending air becomes warmer and drier on the leeward side.
📌 Must-Memorise

Windward → Wet

Leeward → Dry

12. Western Ghats — Orographic Rainfall
  • Arabian Sea monsoon winds strike the Western Ghats.
  • Kerala, coastal Karnataka, Goa and Konkan receive heavy rainfall.
  • Interior Deccan receives much less rainfall because of rain-shadow effects.
13. Khasi Hills — Orographic Rainfall
  • Moist Bay of Bengal winds are forced up the southern slopes of the Khasi Hills.
  • Mawsynram and Cherrapunji receive extremely heavy rainfall.
  • This is one of India's best examples of orographic rainfall.
14. Cyclonic Rainfall
  • Cyclonic rainfall occurs due to convergence and uplift around low-pressure systems.
  • It may be associated with:
  • Depressions.
  • Tropical cyclones.
  • Temperate cyclones.
  • Frontal systems.
15. Frontal Rainfall
  • Frontal rainfall occurs when different air masses meet.
  • Warm air is forced to rise over colder air.
  • Cooling produces condensation and rainfall.
  • Western disturbances produce this type of rainfall over northwestern India.
16. Seasonal Distribution of Rainfall

India receives rainfall mainly from:

  • Southwest monsoon.
  • Northeast monsoon.
  • Western disturbances.
  • Pre-monsoon thunderstorms.
  • Tropical cyclones and depressions.
17. Southwest Monsoon Rainfall
  • June to September is the principal rainy season for most of India.
  • Southwest monsoon contributes the largest share of annual rainfall nationally.
  • Distribution depends heavily on relief and monsoon-system movement.
18. Northeast Monsoon Rainfall
  • Northeast monsoon is especially important from October to December.
  • Tamil Nadu receives a major share of its annual rainfall during this season.
  • Bay of Bengal depressions and cyclones enhance rainfall.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

October–December → Northeast Monsoon Rainfall

19. Winter Rainfall
  • Northwestern India receives some winter rainfall from western disturbances.
  • Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, western Uttar Pradesh and Himalayan regions are affected.
  • Snowfall occurs in the western Himalayas.
20. Pre-Monsoon Rainfall

Important pre-monsoon weather includes:

  • Mango showers.
  • Blossom showers.
  • Kalbaisakhi/Nor'westers.
  • Dust storms.
  • Local thunderstorms.
21. Annual Rainfall Pattern

Broadly:

  • Very high rainfall → Western Ghats and northeast India.
  • High to moderate rainfall → Eastern India and Himalayan foothills.
  • Moderate rainfall → Central India and parts of Ganga Plain.
  • Low rainfall → Interior Deccan and northwestern India.
  • Very low rainfall → Thar Desert and Ladakh.
22. Highest-Rainfall Region
  • Southern Meghalaya is one of the wettest regions of the world.
  • Mawsynram is famous for extremely high average annual rainfall.
  • Cherrapunji/Sohra lies nearby.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mawsynram → Meghalaya → Very High Rainfall

23. Mawsynram — Why So Wet

Reasons include:

  • Moist Bay of Bengal winds.
  • Funnel-shaped relief.
  • Steep southern Khasi Hills.
  • Strong orographic uplift.
24. Cherrapunji / Sohra
  • Sohra lies in Meghalaya.
  • It receives exceptionally heavy rainfall.
  • Despite very high rainfall, dry-season water scarcity can occur because steep slopes and rapid runoff limit storage.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Very High Rainfall ≠ No Water Scarcity

25. Low-Rainfall Region — Rajasthan
  • Western Rajasthan receives very low and highly variable rainfall.
  • Jaisalmer and adjoining desert regions are especially dry.
  • Rainfall decreases generally westward.
26. Low-Rainfall Region — Ladakh
  • Ladakh has a cold-desert climate.
  • It lies in the rain shadow of the Himalayas.
  • Annual precipitation is very low.
27. Rainfall Gradient in Northern Plains
  • Rainfall generally decreases from east to west across the Ganga Plain.
  • Bay of Bengal monsoon winds progressively lose moisture inland.
📌 Must-Memorise

Northern Plains Rainfall → East to West Decrease

28. Rainfall Gradient across Western Ghats
  • Rainfall is very high on western windward slopes.
  • It drops sharply east of the crest.
  • This produces major climatic contrasts across short distances.
29. Rain Shadow of Deccan Plateau

Important low-rainfall interiors include parts of:

  • Maharashtra.
  • Karnataka.
  • Telangana.
  • Tamil Nadu.
30. Tamil Nadu Rainfall Pattern
  • Tamil Nadu differs from most of India.
  • Much of the state lies in the rain shadow of Western Ghats during southwest monsoon.
  • Northeast monsoon therefore becomes especially important.
  • Coastal Tamil Nadu receives heavy rain from Bay of Bengal systems.
31. Tamil Nadu Seasonal Rainfall Sources

Tamil Nadu receives rain from:

  • Southwest monsoon.
  • Northeast monsoon.
  • Pre-monsoon convection.
  • Cyclonic storms and depressions.

The northeast monsoon is especially critical.

32. Tamil Nadu Regional Variation
  • Nilgiris and western highlands receive substantial southwest monsoon rainfall.
  • Eastern coastal districts depend heavily on northeast monsoon.
  • Interior districts are generally drier.
  • Kanyakumari benefits from both monsoons.
33. Coromandel Coast Rainfall
  • Coromandel Coast receives relatively less southwest monsoon rain.
  • It receives its principal seasonal rainfall during October-December.
  • Cyclonic systems frequently enhance rainfall.
34. Rainfall Measurement
  • Rainfall is measured using a rain gauge.
  • It is normally expressed in millimetres.
  • One millimetre of rainfall means one litre of water falling over one square metre.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 mm Rainfall → 1 Litre per m²

35. Isohyet
  • An isohyet is a line joining places receiving equal rainfall.
  • Isohyet maps show spatial rainfall distribution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Isohyet → Equal Rainfall

36. Average Rainfall
  • Average rainfall is usually calculated from observations over many years.
  • Long-term averages are used to identify normal climatic conditions.
37. Rainfall Departure
  • Rainfall departure compares actual rainfall with the long-term normal.
  • Positive departure means above-normal rainfall.
  • Negative departure means below-normal rainfall.
38. Rainfall Variability
  • Variability refers to changes in rainfall from year to year.
  • Arid regions generally have higher relative variability.
  • High variability increases drought risk.
39. Spatial Variability
  • Rainfall can vary sharply between nearby locations.
  • Mountain relief can produce dramatic differences over short distances.
  • Therefore, national rainfall averages may hide severe local deficits or excesses.
40. Temporal Variability

Rainfall may vary in:

  • Onset date.
  • Number of rainy days.
  • Dry-spell duration.
  • Intensity.
  • Withdrawal date.
41. Rainfall Intensity
  • Rainfall intensity means amount of rain falling per unit time.
  • High-intensity rainfall increases:
  • Surface runoff.
  • Flash floods.
  • Soil erosion.
  • Urban flooding.
42. Heavy Rainfall
  • Heavy rainfall may result from:
  • Monsoon depressions.
  • Tropical cyclones.
  • Orographic uplift.
  • Strong convection.
  • Cloudbursts.
43. Cloudburst
  • A cloudburst is extremely intense rainfall over a small area within a short time.
  • Mountainous regions are especially vulnerable.
  • It can trigger flash floods and landslides.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cloudburst → Intense Local Rain → Flash Flood Risk

44. Flash Floods
  • Flash floods develop rapidly.
  • They are caused by intense rainfall, cloudbursts or sudden water release.
  • Mountain valleys and urban areas are particularly vulnerable.
45. Monsoon Depressions
  • Monsoon depressions commonly form over the Bay of Bengal.
  • They move inland toward central and northern India.
  • They are major distributors of monsoon rainfall.
46. Monsoon Low-Pressure Areas
  • Low-pressure areas are generally weaker than depressions.
  • They are more frequent.
  • They also produce widespread monsoon rain.
47. Tropical Cyclones
  • Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure systems over warm tropical oceans.
  • They produce:
  • Strong winds.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Storm surge.
  • Coastal flooding.
48. Bay of Bengal Cyclones
  • Bay of Bengal is especially important for cyclones affecting India.
  • Major vulnerable states include:
  • West Bengal.
  • Odisha.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Tamil Nadu.
49. Arabian Sea Cyclones
  • Cyclones also form over the Arabian Sea.
  • They can affect Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Kerala.
  • Arabian Sea cyclones are important coastal hazards.
50. Cyclone Seasons

Tropical cyclone activity around India is especially notable during:

  • Pre-monsoon period.
  • Post-monsoon period.

The post-monsoon period is particularly important for Tamil Nadu.

51. Cyclone Structure

A mature tropical cyclone includes:

  • Eye.
  • Eyewall.
  • Spiral rainbands.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cyclone Centre → Eye

52. Eye of a Cyclone
  • The eye is the central region.
  • It often has relatively calm winds and less cloud.
  • Atmospheric pressure is lowest near the centre.
53. Eyewall
  • Eyewall surrounds the eye.
  • It contains the strongest winds.
  • Very heavy rainfall occurs there.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Strongest Cyclone Winds → Eyewall, not Eye

54. Spiral Rainbands
  • Spiral rainbands are curved bands of clouds and rain around a cyclone.
  • They can produce heavy rain far from the cyclone centre.
55. Storm Surge
  • Storm surge is an abnormal rise in sea level caused mainly by cyclone winds and low atmospheric pressure.
  • It is often the most destructive coastal hazard associated with cyclones.
  • Low-lying deltaic coasts are highly vulnerable.
📌 Must-Memorise

Storm Surge → Abnormal Sea-Level Rise

56. Cyclone Rotation
  • In the Northern Hemisphere, tropical cyclones rotate anticlockwise.
  • In the Southern Hemisphere, they rotate clockwise.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Northern Hemisphere Cyclone → Anticlockwise

57. Tropical Cyclone Formation Conditions

Favourable conditions include:

  • Warm ocean water.
  • Abundant atmospheric moisture.
  • Low vertical wind shear.
  • Sufficient Coriolis force.
  • Atmospheric instability.
  • Pre-existing disturbance.
58. Warm Sea Requirement
  • Tropical cyclones generally require very warm sea-surface temperatures.
  • Warm water provides heat and moisture to the storm.
  • Energy is released when water vapour condenses.
59. Coriolis and Cyclones
  • Cyclones rarely form exactly at the Equator.
  • Coriolis force is too weak there to provide sufficient rotational effect.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tropical Cyclones → Rare Near Equator

60. Cyclone Weakening

Cyclones weaken when they:

  • Move over land.
  • Pass over cooler water.
  • Encounter strong wind shear.
  • Lose their oceanic moisture supply.
61. Naming of Cyclones
  • Tropical cyclones in the North Indian Ocean are given names from predetermined regional lists.
  • Naming helps communication and public warning.
  • Different countries contribute names to the regional system.
62. Western Disturbances
  • Western disturbances are extratropical weather systems.
  • They move eastward from the Mediterranean-West Asian region.
  • They affect northwestern India mainly during winter.
63. Weather Produced by Western Disturbances

They bring:

  • Winter rain to plains.
  • Snowfall to Himalayas.
  • Cloudy conditions.
  • Temperature changes.
64. Agricultural Importance of Western Disturbances
  • Winter rainfall benefits wheat, mustard and other rabi crops.
  • Excess rainfall or hail can also damage crops.
65. Hailstorms
  • Hail consists of balls or lumps of ice falling from thunderstorms.
  • Hailstorms can cause severe crop damage.
  • They may accompany strong convective weather.
66. Thunderstorms
  • Thunderstorms are associated with cumulonimbus clouds.
  • They may produce:
  • Heavy rain.
  • Lightning.
  • Thunder.
  • Hail.
  • Strong gusty winds.
67. Lightning
  • Lightning is a large electrical discharge within or between clouds or between clouds and ground.
  • It is a major weather hazard in India.
68. Cumulonimbus Cloud
  • Cumulonimbus is a vertically developed thunderstorm cloud.
  • It can extend through much of the troposphere.
  • Severe weather is commonly associated with it.
📌 Must-Memorise

Thunderstorm Cloud → Cumulonimbus

69. Kalbaisakhi
  • Kalbaisakhi are violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms affecting West Bengal and adjoining eastern India.
  • They generally occur during April-May.
  • They are also called Nor'westers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kalbaisakhi → Bengal

70. Nor'westers
  • Nor'westers affect eastern and northeastern India.
  • They may bring strong winds, lightning and heavy rain.
  • They benefit some crops while damaging others.
71. Mango Showers
  • Mango showers are pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka.
  • They help early mango ripening.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mango Showers → Kerala + Karnataka

72. Blossom Showers
  • Blossom showers occur in coffee-growing regions, especially Karnataka.
  • They promote coffee flowering.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Blossom Showers → Coffee

73. Loo
  • Loo is a hot, dry summer wind of northern and northwestern India.
  • It is common in May and June before monsoon arrival.
  • It can cause heat-related illness.
74. Dust Storms
  • Dust storms are frequent in dry northwestern India during the hot season.
  • Strong winds carry large amounts of dust.
  • Visibility can become very poor.
75. Heat Low and Summer Weather
  • Intense summer heating creates low pressure over northwestern India.
  • Dust storms, hot winds and strong convection occur before monsoon onset.
76. Heat Wave
  • A heat wave is a period of unusually high temperature compared with local climatological conditions.
  • Northern, central and interior peninsular India can experience severe heat waves.
77. Cold Wave
  • A cold wave is a spell of unusually low temperature.
  • Northern and northwestern India are particularly vulnerable during winter.
  • Cold continental air and clear skies can intensify cooling.
78. Fog
  • Fog consists of tiny water droplets suspended near the ground.
  • It reduces visibility.
  • Dense winter fog commonly affects the Indo-Gangetic Plain.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Winter Fog → Northern Plains

79. Radiation Fog
  • Radiation fog forms when the ground cools strongly at night.
  • Air close to the ground cools to saturation.
  • Clear skies and light winds favour formation.
80. Winter Fog and Transport

Dense fog can disrupt:

  • Road transport.
  • Railways.
  • Aviation.

It is especially important across northern India.

81. Temperature Inversion
  • Normally, temperature decreases with height.
  • During inversion, cooler air lies near the surface beneath warmer air.
  • Inversions can trap pollutants and enhance fog.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Temperature Inversion → Pollution Trapping

82. Urban Smog and Winter Weather
  • Calm winds and inversion conditions can trap pollutants over cities.
  • Northern Indian cities often experience severe winter air-pollution episodes under such conditions.
83. Frost
  • Frost forms when water vapour deposits or freezes on surfaces below freezing temperature.
  • It can damage crops.
  • Frost occurs mainly in northern and high-altitude regions.
84. Snowfall
  • Snowfall occurs mainly in Himalayan regions.
  • Western disturbances provide significant winter snowfall in the western Himalayas.
  • Snow contributes to glacier accumulation and river flow.
85. Avalanche
  • Avalanches are rapid downslope movements of snow and ice.
  • Heavy snowfall, unstable snow layers and steep slopes increase risk.
  • They affect high Himalayan regions.
86. Weather Systems and Himalayan Hazards

Heavy rainfall or snowfall can trigger:

  • Landslides.
  • Avalanches.
  • Flash floods.
  • Glacial lake outburst floods.
87. Monsoon Trough
  • The monsoon trough is an elongated summer low-pressure zone.
  • Its movement determines where intense rainfall occurs.
  • Southward movement often favours central Indian rain.
88. Himalayan Foothill Rain during Monsoon Break
  • When the monsoon trough shifts northward, rainfall may concentrate along Himalayan foothills.
  • Central India may experience a dry spell.
89. Offshore Trough
  • An offshore trough can develop along the west coast.
  • It enhances rainfall over:
  • Konkan.
  • Goa.
  • Coastal Karnataka.
  • Kerala.
90. Low-Level Jet
  • Strong moist winds at low altitude over the Arabian Sea contribute to heavy west-coast rainfall.
  • The Somali Jet is an important component.
91. Somali Jet
  • Somali Jet flows strongly near the east African coast during summer.
  • It transports moisture across the Arabian Sea toward India.
92. Jet Streams and Weather
  • Upper-level jet streams influence movement of weather systems.
  • The subtropical westerly jet is particularly important for winter weather.
  • Tropical easterly circulation is associated with summer monsoon.
93. Western Disturbance Path
  • Western disturbances generally move from west to east.
  • They enter India through northwestern regions.
  • They then move across northern India and the Himalayas.
94. Monsoon Depression Path
  • Monsoon depressions often form over the northern Bay of Bengal.
  • They commonly move west or northwest across central India.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Western Disturbance → West to East

Monsoon Depression → Often East to West/Northwest

95. Tropical Cyclone vs Western Disturbance

Tropical Cyclone:

  • Tropical ocean origin.
  • Warm-core.
  • Strong winds.
  • Heavy rain and storm surge.

Western Disturbance:

  • Extratropical origin.
  • Westerly circulation.
  • Mainly winter influence.
  • Rain and snow in northwestern India.
96. Cyclone vs Depression
  • Both are low-pressure systems.
  • Cyclones have stronger organised wind circulation.
  • Depressions are weaker but can still produce very heavy rainfall.
97. Rainfall and Floods

Flood risk increases with:

  • Intense rainfall.
  • Saturated soil.
  • High river discharge.
  • Poor drainage.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Encroachment on floodplains.
98. Urban Flooding

Urban floods are intensified by:

  • Impervious surfaces.
  • Blocked drains.
  • Wetland loss.
  • Encroached waterways.
  • Very intense short-duration rain.
99. Chennai Flooding Link
  • Chennai's flat coastal terrain makes drainage difficult during intense rainfall.
  • Northeast monsoon depressions and cyclones can produce very heavy rain.
  • Loss of natural drainage and wetlands can aggravate flooding.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Chennai Flood Risk → NE Monsoon + Cyclonic Rain + Urban Drainage

100. Chennai and Coastal Weather
  • Chennai faces the Bay of Bengal.
  • It experiences high humidity.
  • Major rainfall occurs during the northeast monsoon.
  • Tropical cyclones can produce extreme rainfall.
101. Tamil Nadu Cyclone-Prone Coast

Important vulnerable areas include:

  • Chennai and northern coast.
  • Cuddalore.
  • Nagapattinam.
  • Mayiladuthurai.
  • Ramanathapuram and adjoining sectors depending on cyclone track.
102. Tamil Nadu Delta Rainfall
  • Kaveri delta agriculture depends strongly on northeast monsoon rainfall.
  • Excess rain can cause flooding.
  • Deficient rain can affect paddy cultivation.
103. Tamil Nadu Tanks and Rainfall
  • Traditional tanks capture seasonal runoff.
  • Northeast monsoon rainfall is critical for replenishing them.
  • Tanks support irrigation and groundwater recharge.
104. Rainfall and Groundwater Recharge
  • Moderate, sustained rainfall generally favours infiltration.
  • Very intense rain may produce more runoff and less infiltration.
  • Soil type and land cover strongly influence recharge.
105. Rainfall and Soil Erosion
  • High-intensity rainfall can detach soil particles.
  • Runoff carries soil downslope.
  • Bare slopes are highly vulnerable.
106. Rainfall and Landslides
  • Prolonged or intense rainfall saturates slopes.
  • Soil and rock strength decrease.
  • Landslide risk increases in mountain regions.
107. Western Ghats Landslide Risk
  • Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra hill regions can experience rainfall-triggered landslides.
  • Steep slopes and land-use change can increase vulnerability.
108. Nilgiris and Landslides
  • Nilgiris receive heavy rainfall in some sectors.
  • Steep slopes and weathered material create landslide risk.
  • Intense rainfall can trigger slope failures.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Nilgiris → Rainfall-Induced Landslide Risk

109. Rainfall and Agriculture

Rainfall controls:

  • Sowing.
  • Crop duration.
  • Irrigation need.
  • Soil moisture.
  • Yield.
  • Harvest conditions.
110. Kharif Rainfall Requirement
  • Kharif crops are strongly dependent on southwest monsoon rainfall.
  • Timely onset is important for sowing.
  • Long dry spells can damage crops.
111. Rabi Rainfall
  • Rabi crops rely mainly on stored soil moisture and irrigation.
  • Western disturbance rainfall is useful in northwestern India.
112. Tamil Nadu Samba Paddy Link
  • Seasonal paddy cultivation in Tamil Nadu depends strongly on northeast monsoon rainfall and irrigation availability.
  • Delta regions are particularly sensitive to rainfall and river-water availability.
113. Rainfall and Reservoirs
  • Reservoir storage rises during rainy seasons.
  • Seasonal rainfall influences:
  • Irrigation.
  • Drinking water.
  • Hydropower.
  • Flood management.
114. Rainfall and Hydroelectricity
  • Heavy monsoon rainfall increases reservoir inflows.
  • Mountainous high-rainfall regions have strong hydropower potential.
115. Rainfall and Natural Vegetation

Broad relationship:

  • High rainfall → Dense forests.
  • Moderate rainfall → Deciduous forests.
  • Low rainfall → Thorn and scrub vegetation.
116. Rainfall and Soil Type
  • High rainfall promotes strong leaching.
  • Low rainfall favours accumulation of salts and calcium compounds.
  • Climate is therefore a major soil-forming factor.
117. Rainfall and River Regimes
  • Himalayan rivers receive monsoon rainfall plus snow/glacier melt.
  • Peninsular rivers depend more strongly on seasonal rainfall.
  • River discharge therefore fluctuates more in many peninsular basins.
118. Rainfall and Drought

Deficient rainfall can produce:

  • Meteorological drought.
  • Agricultural drought.
  • Hydrological drought.
  • Socioeconomic impacts.
119. Meteorological Drought
  • Meteorological drought refers to substantial rainfall deficiency relative to normal.
120. Agricultural Drought
  • Agricultural drought occurs when soil moisture is inadequate for crops.
  • Poor rainfall distribution can cause it even when total seasonal rainfall is near normal.
121. Hydrological Drought
  • Hydrological drought involves low:
  • River flows.
  • Reservoir levels.
  • Lake levels.
  • Groundwater levels.
122. Rainfall Deficiency and Desert Areas
  • Rajasthan is particularly vulnerable because rainfall is low and highly variable.
  • Droughts can occur frequently.
123. Rainfall Excess and Flood Areas

High flood susceptibility occurs in:

  • Assam.
  • Bihar.
  • Eastern Uttar Pradesh.
  • West Bengal.
  • Coastal cyclone-prone states.
124. Assam Floods
  • Brahmaputra receives heavy monsoon rainfall.
  • Himalayan tributaries bring high discharge and sediments.
  • Channel migration and bank erosion worsen flood impact.
125. Bihar Floods
  • Himalayan tributaries such as Kosi and Gandak contribute to flooding.
  • Flat terrain and high sediment loads increase vulnerability.
126. Rainfall and Cyclone Storm Surge
  • Cyclones produce both rainfall and storm surge.
  • Flooding may therefore occur from:
  • River runoff.
  • Direct rainfall.
  • Sea-water inundation.
127. Rainfall Forecasting

Meteorologists use:

  • Satellites.
  • Weather radars.
  • Rain gauges.
  • Automatic weather stations.
  • Numerical weather-prediction models.
128. Weather Satellite

Satellites monitor:

  • Clouds.
  • Cyclones.
  • Water vapour.
  • Sea-surface conditions.
  • Large-scale weather systems.
129. Doppler Weather Radar
  • Doppler weather radar tracks precipitation and storm movement.
  • It helps detect:
  • Thunderstorms.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Cyclone rainbands.
  • Wind patterns.
130. Automatic Weather Station
  • Automatic weather stations continuously record meteorological variables.
  • Common measurements include:
  • Temperature.
  • Humidity.
  • Pressure.
  • Wind.
  • Rainfall.
131. Weather Instruments
  • Thermometer → Temperature.
  • Barometer → Pressure.
  • Hygrometer → Humidity.
  • Rain gauge → Rainfall.
  • Anemometer → Wind speed.
  • Wind vane → Wind direction.
132. Beaufort Scale
  • Beaufort scale describes wind force based on wind speed and observed effects.
  • It was developed originally for marine use.
133. Atmospheric Pressure
  • Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted by the weight of air.
  • Weather systems are strongly controlled by pressure differences.
  • Air generally moves from high pressure toward low pressure.
134. Isobar
  • An isobar joins points of equal atmospheric pressure.
  • Closely spaced isobars indicate a strong pressure gradient and stronger winds.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Close Isobars → Strong Winds

135. Pressure Gradient
  • Pressure-gradient force moves air from high pressure toward low pressure.
  • Greater pressure difference over a short distance generally produces stronger winds.
136. Wind Direction around Low Pressure

In the Northern Hemisphere:

  • Air converges toward low pressure.
  • Coriolis force produces anticlockwise circulation.
137. Wind Direction around High Pressure

In the Northern Hemisphere:

  • Air diverges outward.
  • Circulation is generally clockwise.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Northern Hemisphere:

Low → Anticlockwise

High → Clockwise

138. Local Winds

Local weather in India is influenced by:

  • Loo.
  • Sea breeze.
  • Land breeze.
  • Mountain breeze.
  • Valley breeze.
139. Sea Breeze
  • During daytime, land heats faster than sea.
  • Low pressure develops over land.
  • Cooler air flows from sea to land.
  • This is called sea breeze.
📌 Must-Memorise

Day → Sea Breeze → Sea to Land

140. Land Breeze
  • At night, land cools faster than sea.
  • Higher pressure develops over land.
  • Air flows from land to sea.
  • This is called land breeze.
📌 Must-Memorise

Night → Land Breeze → Land to Sea

141. Sea Breeze and Chennai
  • Chennai commonly experiences sea-breeze effects because of its Bay of Bengal coast.
  • Afternoon sea breezes can moderate daytime heat near the coast.
142. Valley Breeze
  • During daytime, mountain slopes heat strongly.
  • Air moves upslope from valleys.
  • This is called valley breeze.
143. Mountain Breeze
  • At night, mountain slopes cool.
  • Dense cold air flows downslope into valleys.
  • This is called mountain breeze.
144. Weather Front
  • A front is the boundary between two different air masses.
  • Fronts are especially important in temperate cyclones.
  • Western disturbances involve frontal weather systems.
145. Warm Front
  • Warm air advances over colder air.
  • It rises gradually.
  • Widespread cloud and steady precipitation can occur.
146. Cold Front
  • Cold air advances beneath warm air.
  • Warm air rises rapidly.
  • Heavy showers and thunderstorms may occur.
147. Air Mass
  • An air mass is a large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and moisture characteristics.
  • Air masses acquire properties from their source regions.
148. Tropical Maritime Air
  • Tropical maritime air is warm and moist.
  • Monsoon winds carry maritime moisture toward India.
149. Continental Air
  • Continental air is generally drier than maritime air.
  • Winter winds over much of India originate over land and are therefore dry.
150. Weather vs Climate

Weather:

  • Short-term.
  • Changes rapidly.
  • Local.

Climate:

  • Long-term.
  • Based on averages and variability.
  • Regional.
151. Tamil Nadu — High-Yield Weather Facts
  • Northeast monsoon is the major rainy season for much of Tamil Nadu.
  • Bay of Bengal cyclones are important rainfall sources.
  • Coromandel Coast is cyclone-prone.
  • Chennai experiences heavy-rainfall and urban-flood risk.
  • Nilgiris face rainfall-induced landslide risk.
  • Palk Bay and Gulf of Mannar coasts can be affected by cyclonic systems.
  • Kanyakumari receives influence from both monsoons.
  • Tank irrigation depends strongly on seasonal rainfall.

154. TNPSC Traps
  • Rainfall is only one form of precipitation.
  • Orographic rainfall occurs on windward slopes.
  • Rain-shadow conditions occur on leeward slopes.
  • Mawsynram's rainfall is mainly orographic.
  • Very high rainfall does not automatically mean year-round water abundance.
  • Northern Plains rainfall generally decreases east to west.
  • Tamil Nadu differs from most of India in seasonal rainfall pattern.
  • Northeast monsoon is critical to Tamil Nadu.
  • One millimetre rainfall equals one litre of water over one square metre.
  • Cloudburst is highly localised and intense.
  • Tropical cyclone eye is relatively calm.
  • Strongest cyclone winds occur in the eyewall.
  • Northern Hemisphere cyclones rotate anticlockwise.
  • Cyclones rarely form at the Equator.
  • Western disturbances are extratropical systems.
  • Kalbaisakhi is a pre-monsoon thunderstorm.
  • Mango shower and blossom shower are not the same.
  • Cumulonimbus is the major thunderstorm cloud.
  • Temperature inversion can trap pollution near the ground.
  • Monsoon depressions and western disturbances have different origins.
  • Chennai's major rainfall season is October-December, not June-September.
  • Nilgiri rainfall can trigger landslides.
  • Closely spaced isobars indicate a strong pressure gradient.
  • Sea breeze occurs during daytime.
  • Land breeze occurs at night.
  • Valley breeze occurs during day.
  • Mountain breeze occurs at night.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is precipitation? → Water falling from the atmosphere in liquid or solid form.
  • Main form of precipitation over most of India? → Rain.
  • Three major rainfall types? → Convectional, orographic and cyclonic rainfall.
  • What causes convectional rainfall? → Strong surface heating and rising air.
  • What causes orographic rainfall? → Moist air forced to rise over mountains.
  • Which side of a mountain receives more rainfall? → Windward side.
  • Which side generally remains dry? → Leeward/rain-shadow side.
  • Classic Indian orographic barrier? → Western Ghats.
  • Another major orographic rainfall region? → Khasi Hills.
  • What is cyclonic rainfall? → Rain associated with low-pressure systems and atmospheric convergence.
  • Western disturbances produce what type of precipitation? → Frontal/cyclonic winter precipitation.
  • Main rainy season for India? → Southwest monsoon, June-September.
  • Main rain season for Tamil Nadu? → Northeast monsoon, October-December.
  • Very wet location in India? → Mawsynram.
  • Mawsynram lies in? → Meghalaya.
  • Cherrapunji is also called? → Sohra.
  • Why are Mawsynram and Sohra very wet? → Orographic uplift of Bay of Bengal winds.
  • Why is western Rajasthan dry? → Continentality, low moisture and weak Aravalli uplift.
  • Why is Ladakh dry? → Himalayan rain shadow.
  • Rainfall across northern plains decreases generally from? → East to west.
  • Instrument used to measure rainfall? → Rain gauge.
  • Unit commonly used? → Millimetre.
  • One millimetre rainfall over one square metre equals? → One litre of water.
  • Line joining equal rainfall? → Isohyet.
  • What is rainfall variability? → Change in rainfall from year to year.
  • What is rainfall intensity? → Rainfall amount per unit time.
  • What is a cloudburst? → Extremely intense rainfall over a small area in a short time.
  • Main consequence of cloudburst? → Flash floods and landslides.
  • Where do many monsoon depressions form? → Bay of Bengal.
  • Which Indian coast is more exposed to Bay cyclones? → Eastern coast.
  • Main east-coast cyclone-prone states? → West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
  • What are the three main parts of a tropical cyclone? → Eye, eyewall and spiral rainbands.
  • Which part of cyclone is relatively calm? → Eye.
  • Where are strongest winds found? → Eyewall.
  • What is storm surge? → Abnormal rise in sea level caused by a cyclone.
  • Cyclone rotation in Northern Hemisphere? → Anticlockwise.
  • Why do tropical cyclones rarely form near the Equator? → Coriolis force is too weak.
  • Cyclones weaken after moving over? → Land or colder water.
  • Western disturbances mainly affect India in which season? → Winter.
  • What do western disturbances bring? → Winter rain and Himalayan snowfall.
  • Which crops benefit from winter rain? → Rabi crops such as wheat and mustard.
  • Thunderstorm cloud? → Cumulonimbus.
  • Pre-monsoon storm of Bengal? → Kalbaisakhi/Nor'wester.
  • Mango showers occur in? → Kerala and Karnataka.
  • Blossom showers are associated with? → Coffee.
  • Hot dry wind of north India? → Loo.
  • Dense winter fog is especially common in? → Indo-Gangetic Plain.
  • What is temperature inversion? → Temperature increases with height over a layer, trapping cold air near the surface.
  • Why can inversion worsen pollution? → It prevents vertical mixing.
  • Monsoon depression movement is commonly? → Westward or northwestward from Bay of Bengal.
  • Western disturbances move generally? → West to east.
  • Offshore trough enhances rainfall along? → Western coast.
  • Somali Jet contributes moisture to which branch? → Arabian Sea branch of southwest monsoon.
  • Major Tamil Nadu flood-producing weather systems? → Northeast monsoon depressions and Bay of Bengal cyclones.
  • Why is Chennai vulnerable to flooding? → Intense northeast-monsoon rain, flat terrain and drainage constraints.
  • Why are Nilgiris vulnerable to landslides? → Steep slopes and intense/prolonged rainfall.
  • What is meteorological drought? → Rainfall deficiency.
  • What is agricultural drought? → Inadequate soil moisture.
  • What is hydrological drought? → Reduced rivers, reservoirs and groundwater.
  • What is a sea breeze? → Daytime wind from sea to land.
  • What is a land breeze? → Nighttime wind from land to sea.
  • What is a valley breeze? → Daytime upslope wind.
  • What is a mountain breeze? → Nighttime downslope wind.
  • What is an isobar? → Line joining equal atmospheric pressure.
  • Closely spaced isobars indicate? → Strong pressure gradient and stronger winds.
  • Low-pressure circulation in Northern Hemisphere? → Anticlockwise.
  • High-pressure circulation in Northern Hemisphere? → Clockwise.
